steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a new OWL ontology embedding method for the description logic EL++ that represents both concepts and roles as boxes. Motivate ontology curation and the limits of symbolic reasoning, review knowledge graph and ontology embedding methods and their shortcomings, and summarize our method and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Ontologies, OWL, Description Logic
- Curating ontologies is hard; symbolic reasoners too rigid
- Knowledge graph embeddings
- Ontology embeddings and their limitations
- Our method and results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Ontologies are a widely used formalism for representing general knowledge about a domain. They are usually specified in the Web Ontology Language (OWL) standard developed by W3C, and they have been widely adopted in many domains like the Semantic Web, healthcare, bioinformatics, and geoinformatics. OWL can express many kinds of statements, from simple relational facts to concept hierarchies and complex logical relationships, and its formal semantics are defined by Description Logic (DL).

Many real-world OWL ontologies have been developed and used with great success, like the Gene Ontology GO and the food ontology FoodOn. But both maintaining these existing OWL ontologies and creating new ones has turned out to be challenging, and it mostly relies on manual work done by experts. Common ontology curation tasks include completing missing subsumptions between concepts (or membership relations between individuals and concepts) and finding missing logical restrictions between concepts. Symbolic logical reasoning algorithms like HermiT and ELK help with this problem by deductively inferring implicit knowledge from the precise semantics of an ontology. However, this classical reasoning is often too rigid for real-world OWL ontologies, especially when the data is incomplete or noisy, and it cannot derive knowledge that is only probable from the given ontology.

At the same time, there has been growing interest in representation learning-based methods for completing Knowledge Graphs (KGs), i.e. relational facts in the form of RDF triples <Subject, Predicate, Object>. Most of these approaches first learn structure-preserving embeddings of the entities and relations (predicates) of a KG in a latent vector space, and then use them to score how likely novel facts are. For example, the classic method TransE maps entities and relations to vectors so that translating the subject embedding by the relation embedding gives approximately the object embedding.

- Ontology embeddings
  - similar techniques for inductive reasoning, complementing deductive reasoning for curation
  - OPA2Vec (cite), OWL2Vec* (cite): textual meta info (labels, comments) for similarity; don't retain DL semantics
  - others embed logical info directly (cite), mostly OWL 2 EL profile (cite), semantics from DL \mathcal{EL^{++}} (cite)
  - ELEm (cite), extension EmEL ++ (cite): concepts as high-dimensional balls; can't capture conjunction (intersection of balls not a ball)
  - -> state of the art BoxEL (cite), ELBE (cite): concepts as boxes (axis-aligned hyperrectangles)
  - all still use TransE (cite) for roles (binary relations) as translations: can't do one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many (cite); limited for role inclusions
  - evaluation only subsumptions between named concepts, no complex concepts / complex logical relationships
- Our method
  - Box {}^{\textsf{2}} EL: OWL ontology embedding for semantics of \mathcal{EL^{++}}, widely adopted in real-life large-scale ontologies (cite)
  - inspired by BoxE (cite): relations and concepts both boxes; concept interactions via bumping mechanism
  - overcomes shortcomings; proven sound (faithfully captures DL semantics) -> theoretical correctness, interpretable inference for completion
  - evaluation: concept subsumption prediction (named and complex), role assertion (link) prediction, approximating deductive reasoning
  - theoretical advantages show in practice; state-of-the-art across datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Ontologies are a widely used formalism for representing general knowledge about a domain. They are usually specified in the Web Ontology Language (OWL) standard developed by W3C, and they have been widely adopted in many domains like the Semantic Web, healthcare, bioinformatics, and geoinformatics. OWL can express many kinds of statements, from simple relational facts to concept hierarchies and complex logical relationships, and its formal semantics are defined by Description Logic (DL).

Many real-world OWL ontologies have been developed and used with great success, like the Gene Ontology GO and the food ontology FoodOn. But both maintaining these existing OWL ontologies and creating new ones has turned out to be challenging, and it mostly relies on manual work done by experts. Common ontology curation tasks include completing missing subsumptions between concepts (or membership relations between individuals and concepts) and finding missing logical restrictions between concepts. Symbolic logical reasoning algorithms like HermiT and ELK help with this problem by deductively inferring implicit knowledge from the precise semantics of an ontology. However, this classical reasoning is often too rigid for real-world OWL ontologies, especially when the data is incomplete or noisy, and it cannot derive knowledge that is only probable from the given ontology.

At the same time, there has been growing interest in representation learning-based methods for completing Knowledge Graphs (KGs), i.e. relational facts in the form of RDF triples <Subject, Predicate, Object>. Most of these approaches first learn structure-preserving embeddings of the entities and relations (predicates) of a KG in a latent vector space, and then use them to score how likely novel facts are. For example, the classic method TransE maps entities and relations to vectors so that translating the subject embedding by the relation embedding gives approximately the object embedding.

Embedding-based techniques similar to the ones for KGs have been developed for inductive reasoning in ontologies, which promises to complement classical deductive reasoning for ontology curation tasks. Some approaches like OPA2Vec and OWL2Vec* exploit textual meta information (e.g., concept labels and comments) to model similarities between entities, but they do not keep the semantics defined by the underlying DL. Other approaches try to embed the logical information of an OWL ontology directly in the latent space, mostly targeting the OWL 2 EL profile, whose semantics are defined by the DL \mathcal{EL^{++}}. Prominent examples are ELEm and its extension EmEL ++, which model concepts as high-dimensional balls. But they cannot faithfully capture concept conjunction, because the intersection of two balls is not a ball anymore. This led to the state-of-the-art methods BoxEL and ELBE, which represent concepts as boxes (i.e., axis-aligned hyperrectangles) instead. However, all of these approaches still use TransE to model roles (i.e., binary relations) as simple translations. TransE cannot capture one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many relationships, and it is limited in how faithfully it can represent inclusion relationships between roles. Also, these current works focus on the basic task of predicting subsumptions between named concepts, and do not consider complex concepts defined with logical operators or complex logical relationships in evaluation.

In this paper, we propose Box {}^{\textsf{2}} EL, a new OWL ontology embedding method that targets the semantics of \mathcal{EL^{++}}, which has been widely adopted in many real-life large-scale ontologies. To address the limitations of existing approaches mentioned above, we take inspiration from BoxE and represent both relations and concepts as boxes, and we model interactions between concepts with a bumping mechanism. We show how Box {}^{\textsf{2}} EL overcomes the shortcomings of previous methods, and we also prove that it is sound, i.e., it faithfully captures the semantics of the underlying DL, which shows it is theoretically correct and supports interpretable inference for ontology completion. We evaluate our method in two different inductive reasoning settings, concept subsumption prediction (with both named and complex concepts) and role assertion (link) prediction, and also on approximating deductive reasoning. Our results show that the theoretical advantages of our approach also show up in practice and give state-of-the-art performance across a variety of datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Ontologies are a widely used formalism to represent general knowledge about a domain [1]. They are usually specified in the Web Ontology Language (OWL) [2] standard developed by W3C, and have been widely adopted in many domains such as the Semantic Web [3], healthcare [4], bioinformatics [5], and geoinformatics [6]. Common ontology curation tasks include completing missing subsumptions between concepts (or membership relations between individuals and concepts) and identifying missing logical restrictions between concepts. Symbolic logical reasoning algorithms such as HermiT [10] and ELK [11] help address this problem by deductively inferring implicit knowledge from the precise semantics of an ontology, but this classical reasoning is often too rigid for real-world OWL ontologies — especially with incomplete or noisy data — and cannot derive knowledge that is only probable from the given ontology.

At the same time, there has been growing interest in representation learning-based methods for completing Knowledge Graphs (KGs) [12], i.e. relational facts in the form of RDF triples <Subject, Predicate, Object>. Most of these approaches first learn structure-preserving embeddings of the entities and relations (predicates) of a KG in a latent vector space and then use them to score the likelihood of novel facts [13]. For example, the classic method TransE [14] maps entities and relations to vectors such that translating the subject embedding by the relation embedding approximately yields the object embedding.

Embedding-based techniques similar to those for KGs have been developed for inductive reasoning in ontologies, promising to complement classical deductive reasoning for ontology curation tasks. Some approaches such as OPA2Vec [15] and OWL2Vec* [16] exploit textual meta information (e.g., concept labels and comments) to model similarities between entities, but do not retain the semantics defined by the underlying DL. Other approaches aim to embed the logical information of an OWL ontology directly in the latent space [17,18,19,20], mostly targeting the OWL 2 EL profile [21], whose semantics are defined according to the DL \mathcal{EL^{++}} [22]. Prominent examples include ELEm [17] and its extension EmEL ++ [18], which model concepts as high-dimensional balls but fail to faithfully capture concept conjunction, since the intersection of two balls is no longer a ball. Furthermore, these works focus on the basic task of predicting subsumptions between named concepts, without considering complex concepts defined with logical operators or complex logical relationships in evaluation.

In this paper, we propose Box {}^{\textsf{2}} EL, a novel OWL ontology embedding method targeting the semantics of \mathcal{EL^{++}}, which has been widely adopted in many real-life large-scale ontologies [25,5]. We not only demonstrate how Box {}^{\textsf{2}} EL overcomes the shortcomings of previous methods, but also prove that it is sound, i.e., faithfully captures the semantics of the underlying DL, which shows its theoretical correctness and supports interpretable inference for ontology completion. We evaluate our method in two different inductive reasoning settings — concept subsumption prediction, involving both named and complex concepts, and role assertion (link) prediction — and on approximating deductive reasoning. Our results demonstrate that the theoretical advantages of our approach manifest in practice and lead to state-of-the-art performance across a variety of datasets.
